spec.name: Alebrije Jaguar-Eagle
spec.description: A Oaxacan alebrije painted-wood fantasy beast: a jaguar-bodied creature with a hooked eagle head and beak, spread feathered wings and a feather-fan tail, covered in dot, flower and leaf patterns in hot folk-art colours.
spec.layout: A jaguar-sized, long-bodied quadruped (about 1.6 m of torso) standing on four paws in a neutral rest pose, facing +Z. From the front (+Z): a hooked eagle beak (upper beak fixed to the head, lower beak on the jaw) at z about 1.45, a big round-eyed feathered head at y about 1.4, two round jaguar ears and a feather crest with a pair of banded horns on top, and a short thick neck with a feather ruff. Behind the neck sit the chest and torso (round, heavy, jaguar-shaped), then the hips and haunches. Wings spread straight out sideways at y about 1.3, each with an arm, a forearm, a hand and a fan of long flight feathers swept back, so the tip-to-tip span is about 3.9 m. Four sturdy legs, all separated and straight: the front legs are jaguar legs with round paws and ivory claws, the hind legs are jaguar thighs with eagle shins and talons, and they stand on y = 0. At the back is a long jaguar tail ending in a fan of feathers (z down to about -1.55), with a ridge of leaf-shaped spines along the spine. Style: painted wood. The base is chunky, faceted and blocky (low segment counts). Every surface is a flat colour, and the character comes from many small separate parts seated on the surface: rows and rings of dots (flattened spheres), jaguar rosettes drawn as a dark ring of dots around an orange or pink centre, stripes, leaf and flower motifs, zig-zag trim, and thin dark outlines. Colours are bright and unmixed and sit side by side with no shading. Warm orange and gold on top; cream, pink and turquoise on the belly and under the wings. The same motifs (dot rosette, five-petal flower, leaf) repeat on every part so the model reads as one painted piece.

parts.builds: The jaguar torso and chest. One smooth-skinned loft over hips, spine1 and spine2: a deep round chest (radius about 0.33 at z 0.5), a slightly narrower waist, and round haunches at the hips (radius about 0.32). The loft runs from z -0.9 to z 0.78, with its axis at y about 0.92 and its top at about y 1.22. It is jaguar orange on the back and sides, with a cream belly and chest bib made as sector bands or separate bands on the underside. It also includes a short neck-stub collar at neckBase (a wide faceted ring in gold, with a zig-zag of small cobalt triangles), and a thin ink outline ring at the waist and at the chest. Painted decoration made as many small separate parts seated on the skin with b.stick, scattered by surface hits: about 12 jaguar rosettes on each flank (a ring of 6 to 7 small ink dots around a hotPink or turquoise centre dot), rows of small cream and gold dots along the flanks, a row of cobalt, lime and coral dots down the belly edge, and two bold five-petal flower motifs (a flower is a gold centre with 5 coral or hotPink flattened-sphere petals) on each shoulder and haunch. A turquoise and gold stripe pair follows the flank line from shoulder to hip. Leaf motifs (flattened green cones) fan around each flower. Includes fur-less 'wood' details: a few small bareWood knots seated on the belly.
parts.attaches: Front end meets the head part's neck at neckBase and chestFront. Wings root at wingRootL and wingRootR on the shoulders. Legs meet at shoulderL, shoulderR, hipL and hipR. The tail meets at tailRoot. The dorsal ridge, built by the tail part, sits on the top between dorsalStart and dorsalEnd.

parts.builds: All four legs, rigid-skinned or smooth over their joint chains, and mirrored with s = ±1. FRONT (jaguar): from shoulderL/R down through elbow and wrist to the paw; thick tapering tubes (radius about 0.13 at the shoulder falling to 0.09 at the wrist), a big rounded paw (a squashed faceted sphere about 0.14 wide x 0.09 tall x 0.2 long) whose lowest point touches y = 0, 4 toes as short capsules at the front of the paw, and 4 curved ivory claws (cones in claw) at the toe tips. Paint: jaguar orange with ink stripe rings at the elbow and wrist, a cream paw cuff of three dots around the wrist, a cobalt zig-zag trim band, and a coral dot per toe. HIND (eagle): a heavy jaguar thigh from hipL/R to kneeL/R (radius about 0.2 falling to 0.12) in orange with 3 rosettes on its outer face, then a feathered 'pantaloon' of 8 to 10 overlapping flat turquoise, cobalt, and gold feather blades hanging from the thigh, then a thin yellow scaly eagle shin (beakYellow, radius about 0.05) from knee to hock and from hock to the foot, with ring segments in ink. Each foot is an eagle talon: 3 forward toes and 1 rear toe, each made of 2 capsule segments in beakYellow with ink joint dots and an ivory curved claw (cone) at the tip, so the toes are separated and spread, resting on y = 0 at talonContactL/R. Small hotPink and lime dots on every toe knuckle. All feet touch the floor, sinking at most 2 cm.
parts.attaches: Front legs start at the shoulder mounts (shoulderL/R) just under the torso. Hind legs start at the hip mounts (hipL/R) and are covered by the torso haunch. Feet end at pawContactFL/FR and talonContactL/R on y = 0.

parts.builds: The eagle head, neck, jaw and every head ornament, built with the head scale constant. NECK: a short thick smooth sweep over neck1 and neck2 from neckBase (radius about 0.2 to 0.17) rising forward to headPivot, painted jaguar orange with cream and a few rosette dots, and a ruff of two overlapping rings of 12 broad pointed feather blades (cobalt, turquoise, gold, hotPink alternating) around neck1. HEAD: a chunky faceted skull (sphere about 0.2 in radius, slightly longer in z) at the head joint, in gold, with a cream throat. UPPER BEAK on the head joint: a strongly hooked beak (a loft or sweep from about z 1.05 down to beakTip at [0, 1.33, 1.45] curving down to a sharp point), beakYellow with a beakTip-coloured tip, ink nostril dots, and a gold and hotPink dot row along the ridge. LOWER BEAK on the jaw joint: a shorter pointed wedge under it (z about 1.0 to 1.38) in beakYellow, with a red tongue (flat forked shape), a row of tiny ivory fangs, and a hotPink gape line. EYES: two large round eyes, one on each side at x about ±0.14, y 1.46, z 1.08, with an ink outline disc, eyeWhite ball, cobalt iris, ink pupil and a tiny white highlight, a heavy gold brow ridge above each (a wedge, with ink outline), and 3 dot-lashes. Concentric dot rings of cobalt, coral and lime around the eyes, and 2 small rosettes on each cheek. EARS: two round jaguar ears (flat faceted discs) on top, orange with ink rim and a cream inner disc. CREST: 7 long feather blades fanned up and back behind the ears (lime, turquoise, hotPink, cobalt, gold, with ink tips). HORNS: two upward-curving banded horns (a sweep with alternating hotPink, cream and turquoise bands and a gold tip) between the ears and crest, with a dot at each band joint. Highest point about y 1.8.
parts.attaches: The neck sweep starts buried in the torso at neckBase (y 1.0, z 0.6). The head sits at headPivot. The jaw rides jawPivot. The beak tip ends at beakTip.

parts.builds: Two outstretched eagle wings, mirrored with s = ±1, spread sideways in the rest pose, each over wingShoulder, wingElbow, wingWrist and wingTip (x up to ±1.95). BONES: a thick smooth wing arm sweep (radius about 0.1 tapering to 0.06) along the chain, painted in jaguar orange with ink rosette dots, and a gold cuff at the elbow and wrist. COVERTS: 3 rows of overlapping rounded feather shapes (extrude with smoothing, thickness about 0.015) over the top of the arm, growing in size from the shoulder outward: the first row small and hotPink, the second turquoise with a cream dot, the third cobalt with a gold dot. Each feather carries a small ink rim shape and a coloured central dot. FLIGHT FEATHERS: 8 long secondaries (about 0.7 m) fanned backward (-z) from the forearm and 6 long primaries (about 0.85 m) fanned from the wrist and hand, each a pointed extruded blade with a separate ink centre stripe and a tip cap, alternating cobalt, gold, leafGreen, hotPink and coral, with cream dot rows down each quill, all in a single plane around y 1.3 and separated so that no two feathers overlap in the same layer. The underside has the same feathers in cream and turquoise (a thin slab sat just below each upper feather). The wing leading edge carries a row of lime and cobalt dots, and a single big flower motif (7 petals around a gold centre) sits at the elbow of each wing. The wing is neutral, level and fully extended, with the finger bones separated.
parts.attaches: Roots at wingRootL and wingRootR on the top-side shoulders of the torso at about y 1.2. Feathers extend outward in +/-X and back in -Z.

parts.builds: TAIL: a long jaguar tail, a smooth sweep over tail1 to tail4 from tailRoot (radius about 0.11 tapering to 0.06) that curves gently up at the end, painted jaguar orange with ink ring stripes every 0.1 m as separate band sweeps, and a row of cream and turquoise dots between the stripes. FAN: at tail4 (tailTip) a fan of 9 long feather blades spread in an arc of about 100 degrees up and back (length about 0.4 m, ending near z -1.55), coloured in turn cobalt, turquoise, gold, hotPink, lime, coral, each with an ink tip, a centre stripe and a cream dot, plus a small purple and gold flower motif at the fan root. DORSAL RIDGE: a row of 9 leaf-shaped spines (extruded leaf outlines, about 0.12 m tall and 0.09 wide) standing along the back from dorsalStart to dorsalEnd on the top of the torso, with the colours cycling leafGreen, turquoise, hotPink, gold and cobalt, and with a small cream dot at the base of each. Between them runs a thin ink line sweep along the spine. Everything sits on the surface of the torso top (y about 1.22) and never enters the head or wing boxes.
parts.attaches: The tail is rooted at tailRoot under the hips. The ridge runs on the torso top between dorsalStart (front) and dorsalEnd (rear).

calls.reasoning:
I'm sketching out the design for an alebrije jaguar-eagle hybrid: a quadruped jaguar body with an eagle head, beak, wings, and feathered tail, decorated with Oaxacan-style dot patterns, facing forward with wings spread at roughly jaguar scale.

I'm breaking the creature into five parts — body (torso, neck base, painted motifs), legs (jaguar front paws, eagle talon hind legs), head (beak, eyes, crest, horns, fangs), wings, and a feathered tail with ornamental dots and flowers — and now working out joint placements starting from the hips and shoulders relative to the floor.

Still mapping out the joint chain...

Finishing up the hind leg joint, then mirroring the naming scheme to L/R suffixes for both front and hind limbs, with hips parenting the hind legs and spine2 parenting the front legs. I'm reasoning that since the full skeleton is built before any part logic runs, the leg builders just need to look up joints by name and construct bone chains from them.

Now I'm sketching wing joints -- shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand positions on each side, keeping the total joint count moderate, and planning to skip separate digit joints in favor of rigid claws on the paw bone while laying out the wing span dimensions.

I'm now plotting the tail curve, placing joints progressively back and upward to form a jaguar-like arc ending around z -1.55, with a feather fan spreading from the final tail joint.

Working out the bounding boxes for each body part: torso, haunches, head, neck, wings, and tail, so each component stays proportioned and properly mounted to the body.

I'll assign the dorsal ridge to the tail part instead—a row of nine painted leaf-spikes running from the base of the neck to the tail base, positioned along the spine top. Legs get the thigh pantaloons, head gets horns, keeping each part's ownership distinct while working out the torso's top height for placement.

Now I'm settling on a limited alebrije palette capped around 24 colors—jaguar orange, gold yellow, dark rosette purple, cream, hot pink, turquoise, deep blue, leaf green, red, violet, beak yellow with a darker tip, white and dark eye tones, black ink, and bare wood.

I'm also working out the attachment points for the rig—neck base, head and jaw pivots, shoulder and hip mounts, wing roots, tail root, and dorsal ridge start/end positions—to keep the body parts properly anchored.

For ownership, the body part handles the torso lofted around spine joints while the neck is skinned by the head part, and the legs part owns thighs and paws with hip-to-knee sweeps. I'm setting a polygon budget across parts (body, legs, head, wings, tail) totaling under 900 to stay within limits.

Now I'm laying out the full joint chain from hips through spine1, spine2, neck1, neck2, to head, defining each joint's position and direction vector to shape the creature's posture.

Continuing down, I'm adding the jaw joint hinged near the beak, then mapping out the front leg chain—shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw—for both sides, plus starting the hind leg structure.

Working out hip, knee, hock, and foot placements for the hind leg, following eagle talon anatomy where the thigh angles down-forward and shin bends down-back before the foot points forward again. Now starting the wing joints off the spine.

Placing the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and tip of the wing with forward-angled directions, confirming the left side uses positive X. Then laying out four tail segments trailing back from the hips, and noting the ears will be round jaguar-style tufts on the head alongside the eagle crest.

For the head I'm designing an eagle skull with a hooked upper beak curving down to a sharp tip and a matching lower beak, round brow-ridged eyes, tiny fangs and a forked red tongue tucked inside the mouth for that alebrije touch, plus spiraled painted horns rising above the ears, a seven-feather crest fanning from the back of the head, a feathered neck ruff, and jaguar rosette spots with a concentric dot motif painted across the face. Now I'm settling on the final color palette.

Every surface in this design should carry painted dots, stripes, and leaf or flower motifs rendered as tiny flattened spheres in contrasting colors over thin outlines, with flat single-color low-poly faceted parts throughout rather than actual paint textures. I need to list out all the mounting points next.

I'm planning the buildTailAndRidge function, using the provided Ctx type as given and mapping out the tail joints with a catmull-rom path through them.

Now I'm working out the tail fan geometry, adjusting blade lengths and angles so the spread stays within the bounding box while pointing up and back from the final tail joint.

Tapering blade length with angle so tips stay within bounds, checking max extents fit the silhouette, and planning slight alternating x-offsets between feathers to avoid z-fighting in the fan.

Now I'm sketching a reusable feather builder function that extrudes a leaf-shaped 2D outline along a length direction and width direction, with a sharp tip and smooth sides, parameterized by position, length, width, and color.

Adding feather dot and stripe helpers...

Still working out the tail geometry...

Computing the cap width generically. Now I'm moving to the dorsal ridge—placing nine leaf spines along the torso's top edge between its start and end points, but I realize I can't reliably query the torso surface since it's built by a different function, so I need another approach.

Settling on a fixed height estimate for the torso top (~1.22, dropping slightly toward the back) and embedding the leaf bases just under that surface. Each leaf will be flat like a fin, oriented with its width along the z-axis and height along y, standing upright with thickness along x.

Still defining leaf shape...

Checking the dorsal taper so the leaf base sits correctly even where the haunch narrows—settling on y≈1.2 with a small sink of about 0.025 so the leaf outline starts slightly recessed into the torso surface.

Finishing the leaf outline with a thin stalk at the base, then placing accent dots along the leaf at various heights. For coloring, I'll cycle through leafGreen, turquoise, hotPink, gold, and cobalt. For the bone attachments, since the joint spec only lists tail1-4 but the ridge runs along the torso, I need to map the ridge to spine joints by z-position instead—using spine2 for the forward section, spine1 for the middle, and hips for the rear.

I'm weighing whether to follow the literal joint spec (tail only) versus what's actually correct for a torso-mounted ridge. Since it's unclear if there's strict validation against the listed joints, I'll prioritize rig correctness and use the spine bones since they're available in J anyway. Now I'm sketching the ink line that sweeps along the dorsal path from start to end.

Adjusting to y-0.005 so the line floats correctly. Now sketching the tail: a catmull curve from the root through several waypoints curving down and back, with tapering radii from 0.115 down to 0.065, noting the tail root sits buried in the jaguar's haunches near the hip joint.

For the tail bone chain, I'll skip including the hips joint since it projects outside the path's start and only tail1 should control the root segment, letting it rotate naturally with the rest of the tail bones. Coloring the tail orange to match, and considering whether the underside near the belly should get a cream tint like the rest of the ventral surface.

Now for the ring stripes, I'm thinking through how to sweep closed ring paths around the tail at regular intervals using the tail path's tangent direction at each point to orient the frame correctly—getting a frame from the point and tangent so the rings sit perpendicular to the tail's curve.

For bone weighting, I'm debating whether to assign rigid bones by z-position per joint segment, or use the tube sweep's own frame which should already carry proper skinned bone weights—the latter seems safer for deformation but I need to check what `frame(at, dir)` actually expects.

Instead, I'll compute ring points manually: center from the path position, tangent for orientation, and perpendicular basis vectors via cross product. For radius, I'll use a simple linear taper function rather than matching the smooth spline exactly, then build an 8-sided circumscribed polygon, accounting for the extra reach of flat faces versus the true radius.

I'm placing the ring bands at roughly every 0.1m along the tail, computing the parametric position for each 0.1 increment from 0.15 to 0.65 along the tail's total length, keeping the ring radius slightly larger than the tail radius so it visibly protrudes without looking absurd.

I'm also adding dots between the rings, alternating cream and turquoise, positioned at angles around the tail's cross-section (near the top and sides) using the sweep frame at each point to orient flattened sphere studs stuck onto the surface.

Tallying up parts: tail body plus 6 rings plus roughly 15 dots gets me to about 22 for the tail alone, then I still need the fan (9 feathers each with tip caps, stripes, and front/back dots, adding up fast) and the flower with its center and petals, so I need to keep a close eye on the total part budget to stay under the limit.

Still working out the budget...

Adding the ridge dots (37 total) brings the running count to 103, plus a gold cuff ring at the fan root brings it to 104. For the leaf ribs, I'm placing a thin rod from base to 0.85H with a protruding cream dot near the base where it crosses the rib.

Now I'm working out the leaf's orientation vectors, picking a perpendicular width axis so the lean angle doesn't distort the cross-section, and checking the cross product gives the correct thickness direction.

For the rib dots, I'm figuring out how to place small flattened spheres along the leaf's face so they protrude slightly as raised bumps rather than floating detached, scaling and offsetting them just enough to sit on the surface.

Now I'm working out the leaf positions along z with even spacing and slightly varying heights using a sine-based bell curve, plus the stalk base y positions interpolating down the stem, and setting up a bone function to assign ridge parts to the right z slice before moving on to placing the fan flower.

For the tail, I'm placing the feather roots buried inside the rounded cap at the tip, sinking them near the center so the visible blade portion starts just outside the cap radius, with the fan converging narrowly at the root and widening further along—accounting for the tail's upward curve at the tip.

Checking the fan spacing, feather width (0.1) actually exceeds the arc spacing between adjacent feathers at mid-length (~0.65L), causing significant overlap—unlike wing feathers where non-overlap is required, fan overlap near the tail tip is natural and expected, though I need to watch for z-fighting between coplanar overlapping blades.

I'll alternate thickness offsets of ±0.008 in x between even/odd feathers so neighboring blades don't occupy the same plane, keeping width around 0.085-0.1 so every-other feather (i, i+2) stays just within spacing tolerance at 0.65L. The small cream accent spheres at each feather's midpoint (radius 0.012) should sit fine within this offset scheme.

Now I'm setting the fan's color cycle across its feathers -- cobalt, turquoise, gold, hotPink, lime, coral, repeating for nine feathers -- with ink-colored stripe and tip details on each, subtle on the cobalt ones but still visible. I'm anchoring the feather bones to tail4's joint direction and positioning each feather's root origin relative to the fan's base offset, then placing a small flower accent near the tail where the fan attaches.

I'm working out the flower motif itself -- a gold center sphere with flattened purple petal spheres arranged in a ring around it, oriented using the local up and forward axes so the petals face outward symmetrically on both sides of the tail near the fan root.

Petals stick out slightly but that's fine. Now I'm placing the gold cuff ring along the tail path, trying to avoid overlap with the flower and other rings by spacing them at different fractions of the tail length, and working out segment distances along the path to find the right position.

I'm alternating tail dot colors between cream and turquoise by angle band, keeping the belly as a cream sector around the bottom. For sticking the decorations onto the body, I'm using a helper with embed and scale parameters so pieces sink partially into the geometry and compress along one axis, relying on default bone attachment since none is specified explicitly.

For the ring details, I'm sweeping a closed Catmull-Rom curve through a small set of points to form a thin tube, picking a low segment count for a faceted look and assigning it an explicit bone since it needs to behave rigidly as a closed loop. I'm also laying out an ink-colored polyline along the spine, adjusting the sample points since the torso height varies along its length.

Now I'm sketching a helper function to build feather geometry from a root position and direction vector.

Still shaping the tip cap geometry...

I'm placing a cream dot on top of the ink stripe at the midpoint, then setting up the rod sweep with hexagonal cross-section. For the fan arrangement, I'm computing each feather's angle incrementally from vertical, tilting slightly backward so the tail tip ends up angled up and back rather than perfectly straight.

Checking the tail tangent direction gives roughly 73°, so I'm narrowing the fan's angular range to stay centered there and recalculating each feather's length so the z-extent doesn't push past the box boundary at -1.6 — adjusting the length formula down slightly to keep the maximum reach just under that limit.

I'll shift the tail root slightly and keep feather widths constant while making center feathers longer, with small alternating x-offsets. For the flower, I'm placing petals in a ring around each side using the axis perpendicular to that face, with purple petals, a gold center, and scaled spheres for a flattened petal shape.

For attaching the flower to the tail, I'm mapping z-ranges to the correct tail bone segments (tail1, tail2, tail3) so the rigid flower part follows the right joint rather than floating between segments.

I'm defining the tapering radius function for the tail sweep, tapering from 0.115 down toward the tip, and checking that the sweep path's centerline and rounded tube corners align with the catmull-rom arc-length parameterization.

Now I'm working out the ring basis vectors at each point along the tail using the tangent and a perpendicular axis, building a 12-point circular ring around the 8-sided tube to decorate it, and sizing that decorative ring relative to the tube's radius so it sits just outside the tube's faceted surface.

Setting up the catmull-rom sweep path with rings at specific distances along the tail (converted to normalized t values), placing dots at ±65 degree angles, and starting to define the leaf outline geometry using half-width measurements for the stalk points.

Positioning the leaf origin slightly below the torso surface so the stalk sinks in naturally, then adding a central rib running partway up the leaf and placing small decorative dots along its width.

I'm setting up the leaf's color cycle (green, turquoise, pink, gold, cobalt) and a slight backward lean, with ink ribs and cream dots layered on top. Now I'm ready to write the actual function, importing THREE and the catmull helper for the curve geometry.

Plotting the tail using catmull spline points that curve gently upward at the end, then placing the feather fan root slightly behind the tail's tip.

I'm planning the buildLegs function using the existing joint objects like shoulder, elbow, wrist, and paw for each leg, working through the front leg positions first using the provided Ctx structure.

For the hind leg, I'm checking that the knee sits forward and the hock sits back relative to hip and foot, so the thigh angles forward-down while the shin angles back-down toward the hock, then to the foot.

I'm deciding to build each segment with capsules or rods using the joint positions directly (since joints already exist as model-space points), passing a `bone` option referencing the joint pair so the mesh deforms with the rig rather than constructing new sweep chains.

Now I'm working out the paw geometry: sizing it as a squashed sphere so its lowest point touches y=0, then tapering the capsule from wrist down to the paw center so it blends smoothly without poking below the ground.

Adding toes as small capsules at the front of the paw, spaced slightly apart, with tiny cone-shaped claws at each tip angled forward-down. Then I'll mirror this whole leg setup for the opposite side.

Now I'm working out the shoulder joint positioning per side and adding decorative ring bands at the elbow and wrist, defining a helper that places a thin torus oriented along the leg's direction, sized to match the tapering leg radius at that point.

Adding zig-zag joint detailing...

For the cream paw cuff, I'm debating between a simple torus band or a few flattened sphere "dots" around the wrist—leaning toward a cream ring with a handful of dots spaced around the visible front half to read as "three dots" without overcomplicating the geometry.

Now I'm writing a helper to place these flattened dot spheres on the limb surface, computing a perpendicular basis from the limb's axis so I can position each dot at a given angle and radius offset from the surface normal.

I'll define v as the cross product of outer lateral and down direction, flipping it so forward stays positive on the z-axis, giving angle 0 as outer face and 90 as forward. Then for the rosette pattern I'm placing a ring of six ink dots surrounding a central dot.

For orienting the rosette on the thigh capsule, I'm using the limb axis as one tangent and the cross product of the surface normal with that axis as the other, then placing dots slightly above the true radius so they sit visibly on the faceted capsule surface without sinking into the flat polygon faces between normals.

I'll go with 10-sided capsules for a chunky low-poly look, accepting that tiny placement errors on the dots will be essentially invisible given the rounded taper caps. For the rosette, I'm planning a ring of 7 small ink dots plus a center pink dot, positioned along the tube's surface.

Rather than approximating, I realize I can place each dot exactly by parameterizing position along the axis and angle around it, using the local radius to convert offsets into proper angular displacement—keeping everything precisely on-surface instead of relying on flat approximation.

Now I need a core surface helper that maps a segment, axial position, and angle to a point and normal, then a dot-placement function that uses it to emit colored parts. With a budget of 190 parts total, I'm carefully allocating counts per limb—rods, paw, toes, claws, ink rings—to stay within that limit.

I'm tallying the part budget across front and hind legs: rosettes, pantaloons, ring segments, toe capsules, knuckle dots, and claws, making sure the totals for each limb multiply out to something that fits inside the 190-part ceiling.

Finishing hind leg count at 54×2=108, then trimming front leg rosettes down to 6 for a total of 64, bringing the full count to 172, safely under the 190 budget — skipping geometry merging for now since it adds complexity. Moving on to defining joint positions for the hind leg: hip, knee, and hock coordinates.

I'm checking that the thigh and shin capsules at each joint stay within the torso bounding box, then sketching thin yellow shin segments with ink rings placed at a couple points along each shin bone.

Now I'm designing feathered pantaloons as leaf-shaped blades hanging from the thigh's outer side, defining a pointed outline and extruding it laterally to give the feathers some volume.

I'm working out how to position each feather's root on the thigh surface, orienting it so one axis wraps around the leg and the other points downward along the hip-to-knee direction, with a slight outward tilt so the feathers flare rather than lying flat.

I'm spacing feathers into rows along the thigh at different heights and angles, planning a top row with wider spread and a second lower row with tighter spacing, alternating colors between them to build layered pantaloons that drape past the knee.

For smoothing, I'll go with 0 and add extra points to stay safe from sharp-corner crossing errors since faceting handles it fine regardless. For feather placement, I need to work out the orientation axes—tangent direction around the curve and the downward direction along the root, building an orthogonal frame rather than assuming perpendicularity.

I'm defining ydir as roughly the down-direction blended with a bit of the outward normal, then deriving x as perpendicular to both via cross product, with the outline hanging in the +y direction and thickness symmetric around x=0. Rigging-wise, feathers attach to the hip bone and stay rigid past the knee, which is fine at rest pose; now moving on to the thin hock/shin bones and feet.

Working out foot placement at (0.3, 0.07, -0.55) with talons made of three forward toes plus one rear toe, each built from two capsule segments of radius 0.022 resting near floor level. I'm laying out the forward toe angles spread at -35°, 0°, and 35° from the forward direction, with segment lengths around 0.1 and 0.08 extending from the ankle point outward and slightly down to suggest a curved claw shape.

Checking the claw cone tip position to make sure it doesn't sink too far below the floor, settling on a downward tilt of -0.45 for a natural curved talon look, and sizing the rear toe with segments of 0.08 and 0.06 extending backward from the ankle, keeping it clear of the box boundary at z -0.95. Now mirroring the forward toe spread symmetrically at roughly ±38°.

Working out the ankle joint and shin geometry, placing the foot point so the shin tapers down to a faceted ankle ball (radius 0.05) whose bottom pole sits flush with the ground plane, using low-poly sphere segments so the flattened bottom touches y=0 cleanly.

Now I'm adding knuckle decoration: small ink dots at each toe joint, plus alternating hotPink and lime accent dots near the base knuckle of every toe, positioning them just above the toe surface so their normals face upward and they read as tiny painted details across all four toes.

Moving up the leg, I'm defining a yellow hock ball with an ink ring accent, then building the shoulder and front upper leg geometry — placing the shoulder capsule where it meets the torso, sizing it to overlap naturally, then continuing down to the elbow and forearm segments toward the wrist, along with ivory curved cone claws on the front paws.
